title: EU Chief Backs Canada as First 'Associate Member'
summary: The European Union's top official has thrown her support behind a plan for Canada to become the bloc's first 'associate member.' Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, told the European Parliament on Wednesday that she wants to work on 'opening the door' for Canada, involving closer ties in key sectors. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in attendance, last week spoke of seeking a 'unique alliance' with the EU. Canada currently faces tense relations with the U.S., compounded by an intensifying trade dispute. Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed last month, sparking new tariffs. President Donald Trump's repeated talk of making Canada the '51st state' has fueled the feud. Von der Leyen said the EU and Canada 'see the world with the same eyes' on topics from AI to climate change and geopolitics. She listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defense, energy, critical minerals, and economic security as key areas for cooperation. However, 'associate membership' does not currently exist, and the process could take years. Some EU countries would prefer to build on existing defense and trade agreements rather than create a new membership category. Ten of the bloc's 27 members have yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago. Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested Ukraine could be granted this new status, to mixed reactions. Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday. Von der Leyen said it was time to bring EU-Canada relations to 'the highest level possible.' The push comes as Canada looks to deepen partnerships beyond its southern neighbor. For now, the idea remains a proposal, with no formal timeline or guarantee that all EU members will agree. Even so, von der Leyen's words signal growing momentum for a closer EU-Canada relationship, and Carney's speech on Thursday could reveal more about what comes next.
why_it_matters: Trade blocs and alliances are being redrawn at a time when old certainties, such as a stable U.S.-Canada friendship, look less reliable — and those shifts will shape jobs, prices and security for today's teenagers.

background_read: The European Union is a club of 27 European countries that share a single market, letting goods, money and people move freely across their borders, and they make many decisions together.

The European Commission (the EU's executive body, which proposes laws and negotiates trade deals) is led by its president, Ursula von der Leyen, who has held the job since 2019; the European Parliament (the EU's directly elected legislature, which she addressed on Wednesday) debates and votes on those proposals.
Canada's prime minister, Mark Carney, took office in 2025, the same year that Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, came to power.

In 2016 Canada and the EU signed a free-trade agreement, but it has only been applied on a temporary basis; national parliaments in several EU countries have still not ratified it, which is why trade deals inside the EU can take many years.
The United States and Canada, long close trading partners, have been locked in a tariff dispute, and President Donald Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state.

perspectives.description: Supporters see an EU-Canada partnership as a way to keep trade flowing and to stand together on AI, climate and defense, especially while relations with the United States are rocky. Von der Leyen says the two 'see the world with the same eyes,' and Canada is looking for partners beyond its southern neighbor.

Some EU governments would rather deepen the defense and trade agreements they already have than invent a new membership category. Expanding the club also raises hard questions about who gets a vote and what obligations an associate member would carry.

The EU has long used tiers of partnership to manage neighbors without offering full membership, and its internal record shows how slowly it moves when 27 parliaments must approve an agreement. The Canada deal signed in 2016 is a live example of that slow machinery.

Nothing is settled: there is no timeline, the status does not legally exist yet, and ten member states still have not ratified the older trade deal. Carney's speech on Thursday could reveal whether Canada wants a symbolic alliance or concrete commitments.
